## Introduction

Prostate carcinoma (PCa) is the second most prevalent form of cancer among men worldwide accounting for 29.4% of cancer cases and is the fifth leading cause of cancer deaths among men (Bray et al. 2024). In spite of this, the most recent Cochrane \[This is a pretty old review from 2013. Consider citing some newer recommendations\] review of prostate cancer screening using prostate-specific antigen (PSA) testing and digital rectal examination (DRE) showed that there was no difference in prostate-cancer specific mortality between screening and control groups. Furthermore, there was a significant increase in moderate-severity harms due to screening including anxiety and bleeding as well as the risk of false-positives with over-diagnosis and over-treatment (Ilic et al. 2013). Therefore, there is a need for both less-invasive and more-accurate screening methods to improve the effectiveness of early screening and to reduce the negative consequences for screening among men.

One potential approach to reduce the false positive rate for early screening and to reduce the risk of harms due to DRE is to employ polygenic hazard scores (PHS) to stratify individuals based on predicted age of onset for prostate cancer (Seibert or another PHS citation). This approach has been shown to accurately predict risk and age of onset for PCa in multiple ethnic groups (Huynh-Le et al. 2021). Furthermore, PHS can be combined with PSA screening and family history to potentially improve the positive predictive value of these screening measures (Seibert et al. 2018). By stratifying individuals using PHS, we can identify individuals who would benefit most through early PSA screening. Stratifying individuals by PHS score could also improve future pharmaceutical studies by identifying individuals with the highest risk of developing prostate cancer.

Currently, few studies have tested published PHS models in populations that differ from the development set. One example of this was the PHS model of Alzheimer's disease from Desikan et al. (2017), which was tested in novel Nordic cohorts from Norway and Denmark (Motazedi 2023). While several PHS models for prostate cancer age-of-diagnosis have been published since 2018 (Seibert, others), to our knowledge, none have been externally validated in other populations that may have missing or imputed SNPs from the model.

In this study, we evaluated the latest published PHS model for individual-level early diagnosis of PCa by performing external validation in Nordic populations. The PHS601 is

Norway offers a unique opportunity for investigating these questions because of their well-developed electronic health records system, which allows investigators to link patient data from disparate health registries including the cancer registry and the death registry.

The most common form of genetic screening in use today is using rare pathogenic variants associated with significantly increased risk. Rare pathogenic variants with large effect sizes are typically considered more useful diagnostically than genetic risk scores consisting of common variants with small effect sizes. Several RPVs PRVs? have been associated with increased risk of prostate cancer diagnosis or associated with worse outcomes including BRCA1 and BRCA2, HOXB13, and MSH1... HOXB13 has the strongest association with prostate cancer, but is rare in the general population at a frequency of 0.1% However, Scandinavian populations have a much higher frequency of this RPV at 1.4% (Seibert). We are interested in investigating if any of these variants could be useful in genetic screening for prostate cancer in Norwegian populations.

### Side Notes

Huynh-LE 2020 and Seibert 2018 say that stratifying individuals by PHS improves the PPV of PSA testing for aggressive/clinically-significant PCa... but aggressive/clinically-significant PCa is partially defined by PSA values \>10. And PHS strata are defined by their increased/earlier risk of PCa. So.. of course peope in the highest quartile of PHS have a higher correlation with PSA? It is not clear to my that that is evidence that stratifying by PHS makes PSA more useful... we already know the individuals in the highest quartile are at increased risk of PCa. But maybe they are arguing that it helps identify *when* we should start screening? Or maybe they argue that people with high PHS *and* high PSA are at increased risk relative to individuals with low PSA or low PHS or both?

In addition, Mohamed et al. 2019 commented on the original Seibert paper criticizing it for 1) not being generalizable to non-European populations and 2) for lacking family history data.

### Clean summary statistics

Summary statistics from previously published PHS models were acquired from the GRS. Each summary statistics file was run through the cleansumstats pipeline to harmonize effect and reference alleles as well as chromosome positions and RSIDs with revision 37 of the 1KG reference panel. ## Discussion

Future Directions

One limitation of this study is the limited sample size of subjects with diagnosis data, age of diagnosis, and metastasis code. If we could get a bigger data set, we could potentially identify additional SNPs specific to the Norwegian population.
